content_list.content_text: By the mid-1920s, cinema, deprived of speech, had already developed a form of visual storytelling as subtle and expressive as words. Although written intertitles stood in for dialogue, it was the images that truly drove the narrative and captured emotions. Free from the demands of sound recording, the camera, which F. W. Murnau (1888-1931) called "the director's paintbrush," achieved a flexibility unsurpassed to this day.
Unable to speak, actors relied on gestures or facial expressions, achieving the same subtlety and depth of feeling they would later attain with the more naturalistic style brought by sound cinema.

quote.quote: Nothing in the world can be compared to the human face. It is a land one can never tire of exploring. There is no greater experience in a studio than to witness the expression of a sensitive face under the mysterious power of inspiration. To see it animated from inside, and turning into poetry.
quote.author: Carl Theodor Dreyer

content_list.content_text: Silence, therefore, was not a limitation. For many aesthetes and film theorists, the uniqueness of film lay precisely in its ability to tell a story through images alone. This quest for a pure cinema found followers in countries as far away as Japan, where the Expressionist Kurutta ippêji (A Page of Madness, 1926), directed by Teinosuke Kinugasa (1896-1982), used only images to tell the disturbing story of events that take place inside an asylum.

Few films went as far as eliminating intertitles completely, but the greatest glory of the final years of silent film undoubtedly lies in its visual refinement. Murnau's Faust (1926), despite its literary origins in the legend of the man who sells his soul to the Devil, is especially notable for its magnificent re-creation of medieval Europe.

information.contentTitle: Janet Gaynor and George O'Brien in Sunrise (1927)
information.contentText: Sunrise is famous for its cinematography and its poignant storytelling.

content_list.content_text: This was one of the most extravagant productions of Universum Film AG (UFA), the largest German studio of the time, which also made the sumptuous Die Nibelungen: Siegfried (1924) and Die Nibelungen: Kriemhilds Rache (Die Nibelungen: Kriemhild's Revenge, 1924), by Fritz Lang (1890-1976), as well as Metropolis (1927), the same director's science fiction epic.

Metropolis, despite its flimsy plot, remains to this day one of the most visually striking evocations of the future ever seen on screen. French cinema aspired to the epic many times, but never as much as in the work of Abel Gance (1889-1981), whose film Napoléon (Napoleon, 1927) took the aesthetic refinement of silent film to the extreme. Danish director Carl Theodor Dreyer (1889-1968) dramatized French history in La passion de Jeanne d'Arc (The Passion of Joan of Arc, 1928), but avoided spectacle as much as possible by focusing obstinately on the emotional registers conveyed by the human face.

content_list.title: The Supreme Work of Master Carl Theodor Dreyer
content_list.description:
The austere Danish master Carl Theodor Dreyer made The Passion of Joan of Arc more than 80 years ago, yet few would deny that his meticulous production still represents a standard of excellence for any character study in cinema.

The film presents the martyrdom of this blend of warrior and maiden, who carries the weight of a nation on her back and does so through an unshakable faith made evident in the expressive power of the protagonist's eyes. This is largely due to the anguished, ethereal performance of the enigmatic Maria Falconetti (1892-1946), a stage actress Dreyer discovered in Paris. (This was not her film debut, however - and, perhaps discouraged by Dreyer's methods, she never made another film.) Falconetti had her suffering, which is palpable on screen, perversely refined, being forced - legend has it - to kneel on stones and to watch the dailies exhaustively until she knew every feature of her face in detail.

Setting the film in the city of Rouen in 1431 and drawing on the manuscripts of Joan's trial, Dreyer works from a palette of raw emotions: Falconetti's expressions proclaim, loud and clear, her character's present agony, past glories and future fears. Often, by framing Joan's face in close-up and at a slightly skewed angle, he sets her sorrow against the monstrous faces of the judges and theologians gathered to force her confession, creating a claustrophobic, desperate atmosphere out of a simple camera movement.

As in later films, among them Vredens dag (Day of Wrath, 1943) and Ordet (1955), Dreyer addresses questions of faith and spirituality by portraying characters who supposedly have reached a state of grace but are judged by a society of skeptics and violent fanatics. The film remains a fascinating anomaly in the history of European cinema.
content_list.credits: Summary based on the text by David Jenkins, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp

content_list.content_text: Indeed, what was most extraordinary about the final period of silent film was its ability to combine visual grandeur with intimacy. This also applies to Hollywood, whose greatest masterpieces were directed by European émigrés. Murnau came from Germany to work for Fox and, in the romantic melodramas Sunrise: A Song of Two Humans (1927) and City Girl (1930), combined stylistic beauty with a delicate attention to human feelings. The Swede Victor Sjöström (1879-1960), known for his studies of rural Scandinavian life, chose an equally remote setting for one of the last great American silent films, The Wind (1928), a powerful melodrama shot on location in the Mojave Desert.

The excellence of silent film in the late 1920s helps explain why many saw the arrival of sound as a step backward. Much of Lonesome (1928), directed by Paul Fejos (1897-1963), another portrait of urban life in the United States made by a European émigré, displays all the refinement of the twilight of that era of cinema, but in it the mood is ruined by terribly banal dialogue sequences.

information.contentText: In this excerpt, known as the "staircase scene," we see the Odessa Steps sequence, beginning with the director's slow-moving camera which, at one point, follows the people, highlighting the despair of men, women and children who have fallen to the ground, being trampled and trying to escape the officers' gunfire. When the authorities begin shooting, in a repugnant massacre that spares neither women nor children, it is hard to contain one's outrage, which motivates the reaction of the sailors of the Potemkin against the authorities shortly afterward. Eisenstein builds the scene carefully, alternating between shots with incredible dynamism and, with great sensitivity, moving us with the images of a mother dying with her son in her arms and of a baby carriage rolling down the steps under fire. And the very composition of the shots, with the soldiers positioned above and the people below on the steps, symbolizes each group's place in the social pyramid that prevailed at the time.

content_list.content_text: Sound opened up new possibilities for cinema and, by the 1930s, the new medium had already secured its place in the United States and Western Europe. However, it would still take years for filmmakers to have the technical means to combine sound with the visual fluency of the last silent films. This is borne out by the exceptional work of the few mature film industries that made this kind of film after 1930.

Until the middle of that decade, Soviet cinema continued to produce great silent films, such as the classic Bronenosets Potyomkin (Battleship Potemkin, 1925), by Sergei M. Eisenstein (1898-1948), one of the most influential directors in the history of cinema. In Japan, where talkies were rare until 1935, filmmakers such as Mikio Naruse (1905-1969) and Hiroshi Shimizu (1903-1966) blended local traditions with the flamboyant style of the Western masters of the late silent era. In films such as Rakudai Wa Shita Keredo (I Flunked, But..., 1932), Yasujiro Ozu (1903-1963) showed that silent film was capable of a realism as authentic as that achieved with sound in the Neorealist films of postwar Italy.
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the text by Alexander Jacoby, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp

movies.title: A Page of Madness
movies.overview: A man takes a job at an asylum with hopes of freeing his imprisoned wife.

movies.original_title: Sunrise: A Song of Two Humans
movies.title: Sunrise: A Song of Two Humans
movies.overview: A married farmer falls under the spell of a slatternly woman from the city, who tries to convince him to drown his wife.

movies.title: Metropolis
movies.overview: In a futuristic city sharply divided between the working class and the city planners, the son of the city's mastermind falls in love with a working class prophet who predicts the coming of a savior to mediate their differences.

movies.title: Napoleon
movies.overview: A massive 5 1/2 hour biopic of Napoleon, tracing his career from his schooldays (where a snowball fight is staged like a military campaign), his flight from Corsica, through the French Revolution (where a real storm is intercut with a political storm) and the Terror, culminating in his triumphant invasion of Italy in 1797 (the film stops there because it was intended to be part one of six, but director Abel Gance never raised the money to make the other five). The film's legendary reputation is due to the astonishing range of techniques that Gance uses to tell his story, culminating in the final twenty-minute triptych sequence, which alternates widescreen panoramas with complex multiple- image montages projected simultaneously on three screens.

movies.title: The Passion of Joan of Arc
movies.overview: A classic of the silent age, this film tells the story of the doomed but ultimately canonized 15th-century teenage warrior. On trial for claiming she'd spoken to God, Jeanne d'Arc is subjected to inhumane treatment and scare tactics at the hands of church court officials. Initially bullied into changing her story, Jeanne eventually opts for what she sees as the truth. Her punishment, a famously brutal execution, earns her perpetual martyrdom.

movies.title: City Girl
movies.overview: A waitress from Chicago falls in love with a man from rural Minnesota and marries him, with the intent of living a better life - but life on the farm has its own challenges.

movies.title: Battleship Potemkin
movies.overview: A dramatized account of a great Russian naval mutiny and a resultant public demonstration, showing support, which brought on a police massacre. The film had an incredible impact on the development of cinema and is a masterful example of montage editing.

movies.title: Pandora's Box
movies.overview: Lulu is a young woman so beautiful and alluring that few can resist her siren charms. The men drawn into her web include respectable newspaper publisher Dr. Ludwig Schön, his musical producer son Alwa, circus performer Rodrigo Quast and Lulu's seedy old friend, Schigolch. When Lulu's charms inevitably lead to tragedy, the downward spiral encompasses them all.

movies.title: October (Ten Days that Shook the World)
movies.overview: Sergei M. Eisenstein's docu-drama about the 1917 October Revolution in Russia. Made ten years after the events and edited in Eisenstein's 'Soviet Montage' style, it re-enacts in celebratory terms several key scenes from the revolution.

movies.title: Strike
movies.overview: The film depicts a strike in 1903 by the workers of a factory in pre-revolutionary Russia, and their subsequent suppression. The film is most famous for a sequence near the end in which the violent putting down of the strike is cross-cut with footage of cattle being slaughtered, although there are several other points in the movie where animals are used as metaphors for the conditions of various individuals. Another theme in the film is collectivism in opposition to individualism which was viewed as a convention of western film.
